subject: paediatrics
title: Pediatric Neuroinfections and Myopathy: TBM, NCC, and Duchenne

steps.tx: Rupture of a subependymal Rich focus into the subarachnoid space discharges tubercle bacilli into basal cerebrospinal fluid. The most catastrophic presentation of childhood tuberculosis is **pediatric tuberculous meningitis** (TBM), characterized by thick gelatinous exudate encasing basal cisterns, circle of Willis arterial adventitia, and cranial nerves. The peak age of incidence is between six months and four years, frequently following primary pulmonary infection.
steps.say: Tuberculous meningitis follows the rupture of a subependymal Rich focus, encasing the brainstem in thick gelatinous exudate. It is the most fatal manifestation of pediatric tuberculosis.

vis.alt: Pathological gross specimen of brain base showing thick gelatinous tuberculous exudate choking cranial nerves and basilar cisterns.
vis.caption: Thick gelatinous basal exudates encasing the optic chiasm, circle of Willis, and cranial nerves in tuberculous meningitis. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Clinical staging according to the British Medical Research Council stratifies severity and prognostic outcome in tuberculous meningitis. In **clinical staging of tuberculous meningitis**, Stage 1 represents early non-specific prodrome with fever, apathy, and irritability without neurological deficits, Stage 2 features meningeal irritation, cranial nerve palsies, and lethargy, and Stage 3 is marked by dense hemiplegia, stupor, decerebrate posturing, and coma.
steps.say: Stage one TBM shows mild irritability without neurological signs. Stage two features cranial nerve palsies and lethargy, while stage three causes dense hemiplegia and coma.

rows: No focal neurological signs, no palsies
Cranial nerve palsies (VI, VII, III), minor deficit
Classic radiological triad on contrast neuroimaging

steps.tx: Basilar arteritis involving lenticulostriate and middle cerebral arterial perforators causes ischemic infarction within deep gray structures. Endarteritis obliterans produces **tuberculous vasculitis with cerebral infarction**, typically affecting the caudate nucleus, anterior thalamus, and anterior limb of the internal capsule, collectively termed the tubercular zone of infarction. Cranial nerve six palsy with lateral rectus weakness is the commonest isolated cranial neuropathy.
steps.say: Endarteritis obliterans of lenticulostriate vessels causes ischemic strokes in the basal ganglia. Abducens sixth nerve palsy is the commonest cranial neuropathy.

left.title: Tubercular Zone of Infarction
points: Endarteritis obliterans affecting perforating vessels
Lenticulostriate and thalamoperforating branches
Bilateral basal ganglia and internal capsule strokes
Presents with acute hemiplegia or movement disorders

right.title: Cranial Nerve Involvement
points: Sixth cranial nerve (abducens) is most common
Third cranial nerve (oculomotor) with ptosis
Seventh cranial nerve (facial) lower motor palsy
Optic nerve involvement causing papilloedema or atrophy

steps.tx: Four-drug antitubercular chemotherapy combined with systemic corticosteroids improves survival and prevents hydrocephalus. Standard treatment for **pediatric tuberculous meningitis therapy** comprises two months of intensive isoniazid, rifampicin, pyrazinamide, and ethambutol, followed by ten months of continuation therapy with isoniazid and rifampicin. Concurrently, oral prednisolone (two to four milligrams per kilogram daily) is administered for four weeks and tapered over four weeks.
steps.say: Treat tuberculous meningitis with four antitubercular drugs for two months, followed by two drugs for ten months. High-dose prednisolone reduces vasculitis and hydrocephalus.

rows: Reduces basilar exudate, arteritis, and edema

steps.tx: Ingestion of Taenia solium pork tapeworm eggs through contaminated food or water leads to larval encystment in the brain. The commonest cause of acquired focal seizures in children across endemic regions is **pediatric neurocysticercosis** (NCC), where oncospheres penetrate the intestinal mucosa and lodge in the cerebral cortex. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging identifies characteristic cystic ring-enhancing lesions with an eccentric hyperdense scolex.
steps.say: Neurocysticercosis is the leading cause of acquired focal seizures in endemic regions, caused by Taenia solium eggs. Neuroimaging reveals ring-enhancing cysts with an eccentric scolex.

vis.alt: Brain MRI displaying vesicular, colloidal, granular-nodular, and calcified stages of neurocysticercosis with scolex.
vis.caption: Brain MRI demonstration of neurocysticercosis exhibiting ring-enhancing parenchymal cysts with an eccentric dot scolex. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Larval cysts progress through predictable evolutionary histopathological stages within the cerebral parenchyma. Beginning as a viable non-inflammatory **vesicular cyst of neurocysticercosis** with a visible larval scolex, host immune recognition triggers degeneration into a colloidal cyst with intense ring enhancement and vasogenic edema, followed by granular-nodular collapse, and terminating in an inactive, calcified punctate granuloma that acts as a chronic epileptogenic focus.
steps.say: Neurocysticercosis evolves from viable vesicular cysts into colloidal ring-enhancing lesions, then granular-nodular nodules, and finally calcified scars causing seizures.

rows: Thin-walled cyst, clear CSF-like fluid, scolex
Degenerating cyst with active host immune reaction
Small nodular ring enhancement, declining edema

steps.tx: Therapeutic cysticidal treatment must always be preceded by corticosteroid administration to suppress inflammatory host responses. In viable or colloidal parenchymal lesions, **albendazole for neurocysticercosis** (fifteen milligrams per kilogram daily in two divided doses for one to two weeks) is co-administered with oral prednisolone to blunt the inflammatory spike induced by parasite death. Anticonvulsant therapy with levetiracetam or carbamazepine controls acute focal convulsions.
steps.say: Always give corticosteroids before starting albendazole to prevent severe cerebral edema from dying parasites. Continue anticonvulsants until the lesion resolves completely.

left.title: Antiparasitic Protocol
points: Oral albendazole 15 mg/kg/day for 7 to 14 days
Or praziquantel 50 mg/kg/day in resistant cases
Co-administer oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day
Start steroid 1 day prior to antiparasitic therapy

right.title: Treatment Contraindications
points: Antiparasitic therapy contraindicated in encephalitis
Contraindicated with massive untreated hydrocephalus
Never treat calcified lesions with cysticidal drugs
Examine fundus to exclude ocular cysticercosis first

steps.tx: X-linked recessive frameshift mutations in the dystrophin gene on chromosome Xp21 abolish cytoskeletal membrane stabilization. Presenting in preschool boys between three and five years, **Duchenne muscular dystrophy** (DMD) results from complete absence of the sarcolemmal structural protein dystrophin. Boys present with frequent falls, waddling gait, difficulty climbing stairs, and marked pseudohypertrophy of the calf muscles due to fibrofatty muscle replacement.
steps.say: Duchenne muscular dystrophy is an X-linked recessive disorder caused by absent dystrophin. Preschool boys present with waddling gait, calf pseudohypertrophy, and frequent falls.

left.title: Clinical Phenotype of DMD
points: Onset between 3 and 5 years with motor clumsiness
Calf pseudohypertrophy (enlarged, firm, rubbery)
Lumbar lordosis and waddling Trendelenburg gait
Serum creatine kinase (CK) elevated 50 to 100-fold

right.title: Genetic Confirmation & Therapy
points: Multiplex ligation-dependent probe amplification (MLPA)
Identifies exonic deletions (65%) or duplications
Prednisolone (0.75 mg/kg/day) prolongs ambulation
Loss of independent ambulation by 10 to 12 years
